Survey year. MTF is a repeated cross-section rather than a panel, so waves are collection occasions and not repeated measures on the same people.
Year of the annual survey administration, 2000-2024.

MTF never releases age in years; the only age items are over/under dichotomies (18 for 12th grade, 16 for 8th/10th). Modal US grade ages assigned as constants, supported by those dichotomies in these data: 54.9% of 12th graders are 18 or older and 56.3% of 10th graders are 16 or older, so each constant sits at the observed boundary. Within-grade variance is zero by construction, so treat as a cohort marker rather than a continuous moderator.

Male/Female are codes 1/2 in every year. 2021 added one merged category 'Other/prefer not to answer' (code 3), which cannot be split and so becomes Unknown; 2022 onward separates Other (3) from Prefer not to answer (4). expression:
coalesce(
  lookup_values(
    race,
    lookup_ethnicity,
    dataset_id = spec$dataset_id,
    target_variable = "ethnicity",
    default = "Unknown"
  ),
  "Unknown"
)
notes: MTF releases only a recoded race variable, and its coding changes in 2005 (0=White/1=Black through 2004, then 1=Black/2=White/3=Hispanic). The tidier resolves that to labels, so the mapping here is a plain shared lookup. Proximate because respondents outside those groups - Asian, American Indian or Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, multiple races - are set to missing in the source rather than released, so Unknown mixes non-response with real non-Black/White/Hispanic respondents. That is 26% of rows in 2000-2004, when no Hispanic category existed at all, and 15% in 2005-2011. The coalesce is required because lookup_values() only applies its default to unmatched non-missing values, so missing race would otherwise stay NA against this row's 'Use Unknown if cannot be derived' rule.

The underlying 2018+ question offers 'American Indian or Alaska Native' and 'Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander', but only the Black/White/Hispanic recode is released; those respondents are folded into missing, so indigenous status cannot be recovered.

Derived from the same recoded race variable as ethnicity, with White as the US majority group. Proximate for the same reason: respondents outside Black/White/Hispanic are missing in the source, so Unknown includes minority respondents who cannot be identified.

MTF has collected no household income, affluence or wealth item in these 25 years. Parental education is the only SES signal available and is reported on its own rows (maternal_education, paternal_education, parental_education) rather than being re-badged as household SES.

Sampling-frame metropolitan status, not a residential self-description: the only urbanicity flag MTF releases for the whole series is whether the school sits inside a Metropolitan Statistical Area. MTF surveys grades 8, 10 and 12; the grade is fixed by which sample the respondent belongs to rather than self-reported, so it is never missing.
Every MTF time-use item is a banded response set, never open-ended hours.
Bespoke MTF time-use items; not drawn from a named instrument.
MTF is a self-completed in-school questionnaire.

Two different items spliced at 2018, which is why this is partial rather than compatible. 2000-2017: 'How much TV do you estimate you watch on an average WEEKDAY?', television only. 2018-2024: 'How many hours do you estimate you watch video, TV, or movies on an electronic device (such as a TV, computer, tablet or smartphone)? a. On an average WEEKDAY?', which covers streaming on any device. The two never overlap in time, so the coalesce is unambiguous, but the construct widens in 2018 and trends across that break should not be read as behaviour change. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change. The pre-2018 weekday item is also more compressed than its weekend counterpart, topping out at '5 hours or more' against '9 hours or more'.

Same 2018 item change as st_watch_wd. The pre-2018 weekend item asks about 'an average WEEKEND (both Saturday and Sunday combined)', so it is halved to give an average weekend day; the 2018+ item already asks about 'an average WEEKEND DAY' and is used as is. The pre-2018 weekend item was only asked in the 8th/10th grade samples, so 12th grade is missing here for 2000-2017. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change.

Project 5:2 weekday/weekend-day weighted mean of st_watch_wd and st_watch_we. Missing wherever the weekend item is missing, which means all 12th grade rows for 2000-2017; st_watch_wd still covers those. Partial for the same 2018 item change as its components. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change.

Device-agnostic gaming item, consistent across the 2018 redesign: 'About how many hours a week do you spend playing electronic games on a computer, TV, phone, or other device?' (2008-2017, weekly, divided by 7) and 'About how many hours on an average DAY do you spend ... playing games on a computer, tv, phone, or other device?' (2018-2024). Not asked before 2008. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change.

The 'doing other things' part of the computer battery is not gaming-free - gaming on a computer falls inside it - and there is no separate item to subtract, so non-gaming computer time cannot be isolated.

Sum of the three parts of the weekly computer battery - 'About how many hours a week do you spend using a computer ... A: doing schoolwork? B: at your job, if you have one? C: doing other things?' - converted to an average day. Restricted to 2000-2012 because the job and other-things parts were dropped after 2012, and summing the schoolwork part alone would understate total computer use. Partial because summing three banded midpoints compounds the banding error and top-coding. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it.

Texting only: 'About how many hours a week do you spend texting on a cell phone?' (2010-2017, weekly, divided by 7) and 'About how many hours on an average DAY do you spend ... texting?' (2018-2024). Partial, and a substantial undercount of the schema construct - MTF has no total-smartphone-time item, and its companion voice-calling item was excluded because talking on the phone is not screen use. Do not pool with studies that measure total smartphone time without accounting for that. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change.

'About how many hours a week do you spend ... visiting social networking sites like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, etc?' (2013-2017, weekly, divided by 7) and the same item asked per average day from 2018. Content-based and independent of st_phone, as the schema requires. Not asked before 2013. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary (e.g. gaming 1.53 h/day in 2017 against 3.28 in 2018) and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion: the 2017 modal answer is '3-5 hours a week' where the 2018 modal answer is '1-2 hours a day'. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments and do not read the step as behaviour change.

'About how many hours a week do you spend using a computer ... A: doing schoolwork?' (2000-2017), converted to an average day. Partial because the schema asks for educational screen use on any device while MTF asks about computers only, so study on a tablet or phone is not counted. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it.

'Not counting work for school or a job, about how many hours a week do you spend on the Internet e-mailing, instant messaging, gaming, shopping, searching, downloading music, etc.?' (2006-2017), converted to an average day. Partial because the item deliberately excludes school and job internet use, whereas the schema asks for internet use for unspecified purposes, and because it bundles activities that later years ask about separately. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it.

'About how many hours a week do you spend ... video chatting (Skype, etc.)?' (2013-2017, weekly, divided by 7) and the same item asked per average day from 2018. Not asked before 2013. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it. IMPORTANT: MTF switched this battery from 'hours a week' to 'hours on an average DAY' in 2018, and the per-day framing elicits far larger estimates. Mean harmonised hours roughly double at that boundary and the jump is present in the raw response distributions, not introduced by the conversion. Treat 2000-2017 and 2018-2024 as different instruments.

'About how many hours on an average DAY do you spend ... emailing?', 2018-2024 only. Before 2018 emailing was named inside the general internet item and cannot be separated from it, so earlier years are missing rather than zero. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it.

'About how many hours on an average DAY do you spend ... shopping online?', 2018-2024 only. Before 2018 shopping was named inside the general internet item and cannot be separated from it, so earlier years are missing rather than zero. Closed bands scored at their midpoint; the open top band is scored as if it had the same width as the band below it.

The nearest item asks about hours a week using a computer 'doing schoolwork', which is educational use in any location (mapped to st_educational), not computer use while at school. MTF measures nothing in the school context.
MTF's internet item explicitly excludes 'work for school or a job', so it is the opposite of school-context internet use. Mapped to st_internet instead.

'Which one of the following best describes your average grade in this school year?', self-reported, asked in every year and grade. Source labels carry the percentage anchors, e.g. 9 = 'A (93-100)' and 1 = 'D (69 or below)'. The -9 missing code has no branch and so becomes NA.

MTF asks how many hours a week are spent on homework, not how often the student completes the homework they are set. Hours cannot be turned into the Always/Usually/Sometimes/Never frequency the schema declares without inventing a threshold.

The same self-reported average grade on the standard US 4.0 grade point scale (A = 4.0, A- = 3.7, ... D = 1.0). Higher is better, as the schema requires; no reversal needed. This is a within-country conversion of letter grades to their own grade point metric, not a conversion between national grading scales.

'How often do you ... feel bullied at school?', 1 = Never through 5 = Every day, asked 2018-2024 only. Dichotomised at any occurrence, matching how BPIPD-1528 maps the HBSC bullying items; that yields 24-39% TRUE depending on grade. Proximate because MTF asks about feeling bullied with no reference period, where the schema specifies being bullied by other students in the past few months. The companion online-bullying item is not mapped here because the schema row is specific to bullying by other students.

'How often do you ... feel bullied online?', 1 = Never through 5 = Every day, asked 2018-2024 only. Dichotomised at any occurrence, matching the threshold used for beh_beenbullied and how BPIPD-1528 maps the HBSC bullying items. Proximate because MTF asks about feeling bullied with no reference period.

'During the LAST 12 MONTHS, how often have you ... taken part in a fight where a group of your friends were against another group?', dichotomised at any occurrence to match BPIPD-1528. Partial because it captures group fighting only, so one-on-one fights are counted as FALSE; prevalence is 15-20%. The -9 missing code has no branch and so becomes NA.

MTF fields a four-item depressive affect battery ('I enjoy life as much as anyone', 'Life often seems meaningless', 'It feels good to be alive', 'The future often seems hopeless') plus a separate loneliness item, on a 1-5 agreement scale, in both grades in all 25 years. These are MTF's own items, not an SCL-90-R subscale or one of its short forms, so they cannot be scored onto this row, and no generic self-report depression row exists to hold them. The items remain in the tidied table if one is added later.

MTF's life satisfaction item is a 7-point satisfaction scale, not the 0-10 Cantril ladder of the best and worst possible life, and rescaling one onto the other would misrepresent both. Mapped to wb_lifesat_singleitem_self instead.

'How satisfied are you with ... your life as a whole these days?' on a 7-point scale anchored 1 = Completely dissatisfied, 4 = Neutral, 7 = Completely satisfied; only points 1, 4 and 7 are labelled. Asked of 12th graders in every year 2000-2024 and never of 8th or 10th graders. The -9 missing code used up to 2011 is cleared to NA.

MTF carries only 4 of the 10 Rosenberg items, on a 5-point agreement scale rather than the standard 4-point, so the 10-40 total this row declares cannot be produced without fabricating the six missing items. Scored on wb_selfesteem_self instead, with the scale recorded in wb_selfesteem_measure.

Sum of the four Rosenberg items MTF carries: 'I take a positive attitude toward myself', 'I feel I am a person of worth, at least on an equal plane with others', 'On the whole, I'm satisfied with myself', and the reverse-worded 'I feel I do not have much to be proud of', which is reversed here as 6 - x. Items score 1 = Disagree to 5 = Agree, so the total runs 4-20 with higher meaning greater self-esteem. All four items are required: a respondent missing any one scores NA rather than a partial total. The -9 missing code used up to 2011 is cleared first so it cannot enter the sum. Partial because this is 4 of the 10 Rosenberg items on a 5-point rather than the standard 4-point response scale, so it is not interchangeable with a full Rosenberg total; see wb_selfesteem_measure and standardise within dataset at analysis.
